title: I no longer care to work on any Ruby gems so I've archived all my repositories
titleZh: I no longer care to work on any Ruby gems so I've archived all my repositories
author: phoronixrly
relevanceReason: 命中 1 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: I’ve decided to archive the source code of my Ruby gems to make it clear that I’m no longer working on them; I’ve written this post to link from them in order to explain why.
In an article published in 2000, Yukihiro Matsumoto (a.k.a. “Matz”), designer of Ruby, wrote,
For me, the purpose of life is, at least partly, to have joy. Programmers often feel joy when they can concentrate on the creative side of programming, so Ruby is designed to make programmers happy.
And as recently as a 2019 interview, he said,
I designed Ruby for humans, not for machines.

comments.author: ttul
comments.textRawHtml:
I was chatting with a friend who commits on a very well known open source project (~80K stars). He is disillusioned not because the robots aren't good at what they do -- they totally are. The sad thing is that he enjoyed writing code and working with the community on improvements because it was a very human, collaborative thing to do. So, while the robots are great at pushing the project forward even faster and doing fantastic things for security and performance, the joy is gone.

I can totally identify with that feeling. It must be how professional mathematicians are feeling as well.

children.author: rco8786
children.textRawHtml:
Everyone in SWE (who got into it for the love of writing code) is experiencing this. I've been direct with my team about it being a legitimate feeling of grief and the grieving process that comes along with it. It's been helpful for folks to hear that they aren't alone in that feeling.

And also that on the other side of that grief is something new and potentially exciting, but very different than what we're all used to.

children.author: JohnBooty
children.textRawHtml:
Like many, I became a SWE because I loved writing code. Ruby, in particular (whatever one thinks of its other strengths and weaknesses) can be very expressive and beautiful.

However, most code is corporate CRUD stuff. The world sort of runs on CRUD. But it's rarely particularly fun, or beautiful, or fulfilling. It tends to be pretty ugly because there's rarely time to make it beautiful. So I'm not losing much joy there.

Additionally, even with an agentic workflow, my team still thinks deeply about architecture issues. We believe that well structured code is better for bots and humans alike. So I am still exercising my engineering brain; I'm writing blueprints and supervising the bricklayers now instead of laying bricks.

Does that match your teams' experience at all? Sometimes I feel like folks on these threads are working in a parallel universe where the majority of coding tasks and somehow fulfilling and fun and not 99% tweaking reports, trying to implement arcane and contradictory business logic, or fighting with shitty and frustrating externalities. Maybe people found joy in those aspects. I guess there are all types of people in the world. I mean, I'm a sicko who loves writing SQL, something that most coders seem to hate.

    I've been direct with my team about it being a legitimate 
    feeling of grief and the grieving process that comes along 
    with it. It's been helpful for folks to hear that they aren't 
    alone in that feeling.
This is super great. God, I wish all leaders had half this much empathy! Good on you.

children.author: ASalazarMX
children.textRawHtml:
I am one of those weirdos that found joy in business software. The clear specifications, reasonable timelines, and enough technical freedom, let you focus on clean, secure, resilient architectures.

I find that I struggle more with personal projects, as I tend to take things where I'm not even in the skirts of the learning curve, and consequently redo my work a few times.

children.author: wincy
children.textRawHtml: Different person but I’ve been a SWE about ten years now - my favorite work has been improving the CRUD stuff people have left behind. Like the time I took a proprietary document they were using to document their REST apis and wrote a converter to turn those into OpenAI spec compliant yaml files, taking a single tenant application and making it a secure multienant application so instead of 80 different app services we had two, coalescing all their data sources into one normalized DB. There’s a lot of work I’ve done I’m really proud of. I’ve always found myself being the “in the muck” guy fixing up and bettering legacy code, I’ve always felt that was really rewarding and interesting.

children.author: JohnBooty
children.textRawHtml:
Thats badass! I like doing that kind of work, but I got very jaded about it over the years, because management generally acted as if the engineers took a shit on the conference table in the middle of a Zoom call with their most important customer whenever anybody attempted to address technical debt, as opposed to delivering more more more features. Unless it was billable agency work, in which case they’d hate it even more.

With massive amounts of effort and strong communication it was usually possible to get some tech debt time, but management acted like they were doing YOU a huge favor. It was kind of a career killer, generally.

Alternatively it was possible to get this kind of work done on my own time… but that’s a marriage killer instead of a career killer.

I burned out on trying after decades.

children.author: tharkun__
children.textRawHtml:
The fun thing is: I don't think this will change that much with AI in the mix ;)

Shitty devs without AI are slowly building BS that wants to be cleaned up.

Shitty devs with AI are much more fasterly building BS that wants to be cleaned up.

I have a similar experience as yours, just add another 10-ish years to the timeline. Literally my first job out of uni, I got to work on a legacy code base that was another 15 years older than that which had a ton of reports all built differently over time with slight variations in both code and end user output that really all wanted to be "the same" both on the code and end user side. So I slowly but surely, one user/PM requested change at a time would build out a common layer of abstractions and shared code that both made the code shared and easier to maintain (great for me!) and consistent for users (great for the PM/users).

Heck, I built a rudimentary TransactSQL parser that'd output stored procedure call graphs to graphviz and then I printed it and hung it on the wall to get through all this and having an LLM to just make a mermaid out of this in 5-ish minutes would definitively have been faster than I was ;)

With an LLM all of that would just have been faster to do but still worthwhile and useful on both levels. I.e. both code abstraction/reuse and PM/user level. Similarly there was a report that one of the devs had to actually run manually and it took him a full week, so users that wanted the report would only request it once a year-ish. When I was asked to learn how to run it from him I was appalled and just took that week to put it into a script that we ran and emailed the report out once a month automatically. They ran that report manually like that for like 10 years prior to that :mindblown:

None of this is an "AI thing". It's a good dev vs. not so good dev thing. And none of it really has to do with coding as in "writing source code" as much as "solving problems for humans" somehow and the "language" you do that in changes over time. If you're the guy that's tied up with the particular language: yeah LLMs are gonna eat your lunch. If you're the problem solver type that uses whatever tools they have available, you're still in demand.

children.author: JohnBooty
children.textRawHtml:
It's a shame, because there is money in it. It's just (like most sensible preventative maintenance) that the financial benefits are typically delayed. And when it comes to software, they're notoriously impossible to quantify.

Generally the only way to get it done in a corpo environment (and receive any kind of thanks or glory, as opposed to just torpedoing your own career) is to let things get so bad that production stability suffers and/or the team's ability to ship features is severely impacted.

...I realize I'm basically just echoing what you said, except more verbose. I'm venting!

children.author: ASalazarMX
children.textRawHtml:
About 80% of the time. It wasn't all about setting a new foundation, even making the existing one solid enough so you can have time to refactor the cruft was enjoyable. I had more trouble in my youth, as I didn't understand why the business didn't change to accommodate my 'masterpieces', and I'd like to think I started enjoying it more as I became wiser.

Disclaimer: I had to take an opportunity at management in cybersecurity, and haven't coded in about five years. It helps a lot when talking to developers about risk mitigation, though.

children.author: adjejmxbdjdn
children.textRawHtml:
I’ve enjoyed it too.

One of the fun things to do would be to use the 8 hrs of work to spend about 4-5 hrs working on deliverables, which was usually sufficient to exceed expectations, using 2-3 of the remaining hours (I’d keep 1-2 hrs for myself), to make significant architectural improvements.

I’d bring in an improvement every 6 months or so and suddenly the app would get significantly better and I’d get credit for it.

children.author: ASalazarMX
children.textRawHtml:
Sorry for the delay. Mostly midrange (AS/400) consulting at manufacturing plants, then full time jobs at a heavy machine dealership, and a bank. Changed to PC development after about 15 years of that, then management, and it hasn't been the same after that, ha ha.

I think the technical freedom plays a big part, not because you're chasing the shiniest, but because you're choosing the tools that will hopefully outlast you. One of my former employers was 'modernizing' their IBM i (former AS/400) systems by porting them to Java and Windows Servers, and they were having all kinds of problems. Couldn't even get the EBCDIC to Unicode conversion quite right. I was lucky not to be there anymore.

children.author: JohnBooty
children.textRawHtml:
I smile whenever I see EBCDIC, probably because I never had to deal with it.

But I'm sorta old and some of my school's texts were outdated so they had programming examples and explanatory text that treated EBCDIC on equal footing with ASCII.

So unlike anybody who dealt with EBCDIC conversions in the wild, seeing that acronym actually takes me back to happier days!
